**File:** `core/src/map/builder.ts`

**Module note** (line 297): rewritten bottom-up when the module is *covered* — every file in it has a fresh note and every child module already has a note — **and** its composite hash changed. The hash is `sha1` of all child file hashes (from their notes) plus all child module hashes (built incrementally in the loop). So a module note rewrites when any file directly in it or in a descendant module changed.

**Project note** (line 321): rewritten when the root module (`''`) has a note **and** the project hash changed. The project hash is `sha1` of every module's path+hash pair. So it rewrites when any module note was written in this build.

Here's what happens, step by step:

### When the model's answer does not parse

`forcedJson` (the function that calls the model and parses the JSON) **returns `null` on any failure** — parse error, empty content, or server refusal. It swallows all errors so the gate never blocks the turn.

The builder's `askAgain` method then **retries once**:
- It appends `BRIEFER` to the last message: *"Answer more briefly: one sentence per field, fewer items."*
- It increases the token budget by 1.5× (`RETRY_GROWTH = 1.5`)
- If the retry also returns `null`, the note is treated as failed

This retry only happens when the build hasn't been aborted — if the user stops the build mid-way, no retry is attempted.

### How the person finds out which notes failed

The `MapBuildResult` carries a `failed: string[]` array that collects every path the model couldn't produce a note for. At the end of the build, the final progress report appends a summary to the message:

```
X file notes, Y module notes; 2 failed (core/src/map/builder.ts, core/src/map/skeleton.ts, …)
```

The `MapTab` UI surfaces this in two ways:

1. **A toast notification** — on `phase === 'done'`, a success toast shows the full message including the failed count and the first three paths (truncated with `…, …` if there are more).
2. **The tree view** — files that never got a note (or whose note's hash no longer matches the source) appear in the tree with a `"stale"` or `"no note"` label in faint text, so the person can see exactly which ones are missing.

A full build failure (an exception during the build itself, not individual note parse failures) flips the phase to `'failed'` and shows an error toast titled *"The map build failed"* with the exception message.

Here's the full lifecycle of the task contract, with the files that matter.

---

### 1. When it's made — `core/src/session/session.ts` (~line 2711)

Before the model says a word on a task-shaped request, `session.ts` calls `distillContract()` (from `contract.ts`). The trigger is:

```ts
// session.ts:2706
if (this.gateProfile !== 'off' && (sendOpts?.distill ?? looksLikeTask(text)) && looksLikeTask(text)) {
  const contract = await distillContract(
    this.opts.client, this.transcript.messages(), userText, signal, this.stepSchemas(),
    { lean: this.gateProfile === 'fast' },
  )
```

`distillContract()` in **`core/src/session/contract.ts`** (line 251) is a forced-JSON generation — the model cannot decline to produce it. It extracts `goal`, `criteria`, `constraints`, `kind`, `changesCode`, and optionally `interfaces` from the user's words. The original request text is saved onto the contract (`contract.request = userText`) so the understanding check can re-read the source, not just the summary.

---

### 2. Where it lands in the transcript — `core/src/session/session.ts` (~line 2732)

The rendered contract is folded **into the user message itself**, not appended as a separate message:

```ts
// session.ts:2732
turnText = `[${renderContract(contract)}]\n\n${promptText}`
```

`renderContract()` (contract.ts:772) formats it as a plain-text block — goal, numbered criteria, constraints, agreed seams, and (after the first acceptance check) the `checkedState` line showing where each criterion stands. This keeps the contract inside the conversation tail where it's visible to the model on every subsequent turn.

---

### 3. How it survives compaction — three layers

**Layer 1 — on-disk persistence.** `SessionMeta` in **`core/src/session/store.ts`** (line 17–20) carries the contract as a field:

```ts
contract?: import('./contract.js').TaskContract
```

`saveMeta()` (store.ts:265) writes the whole `SessionMeta` — including `contract` — to `<id>.meta.json`. On session resume, `load()` (store.ts:220) reads it back verbatim.

**Layer 2 — re-promotion into the system prompt at every swap.** `applyCompactionSwap()` in `session.ts` (line 3866) rebuilds message 0 from scratch via `buildSystemPrompt()` (imported from **`core/src/agent/prompt.ts`**). The contract is passed in explicitly:

```ts
// session.ts:3819
...(this.meta.contract !== undefined && this.meta.contract.satisfied !== true
  ? { contract: renderContract(this.meta.contract) } : {}),
```

`buildSystemPrompt()` in `prompt.ts` (line 320) appends it to the system message body:

```ts
if (opts.contract !== undefined && opts.contract !== '') parts.push('', opts.contract)
```

So after every compaction swap, message 0 carries the contract again — not the tail note that announced it (which is usually in the summarised middle and gone), but the live, up-to-date version with the latest `checkedState`.

**Layer 3 — the acceptance gate keeps it alive between swaps.** `acceptanceGate()` (session.ts:1173) runs `checkAcceptance()` (contract.ts:1232) at the end of every writing turn. The report's verdict is written back onto the contract (`contract.checkedState = renderCheckedState(...)`) and persisted via `saveMeta()`. So the contract on disk is always the latest audit, and the next compaction swap promotes that fresh state into message 0.

---

### Files, in order of responsibility

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `core/src/session/contract.ts` | `TaskContract` interface, `distillContract()`, `renderContract()`, `checkAcceptance()`, `renderCheckedState()` |
| `core/src/session/session.ts` | Triggers distillation before the turn, folds contract into the user message, re-promotes it in `applyCompactionSwap()` and `previewContext()`, enforces it in `acceptanceGate()` |
| `core/src/session/store.ts` | `SessionMeta.contract` field, `saveMeta()` / `load()` — the on-disk home that survives process restart and every compaction |
| `core/src/agent/prompt.ts` | `buildSystemPrompt()` — the function that actually appends the rendered contract into message 0 on every swap |

The file is **`core/src/session/slot-record.ts`**.

Here's how it works and why there's exactly one file per workspace:

### How the app decides which session resumes

When a session starts, `session.ts` calls `restoreSlot()` (line 4324), which:

1. Reads the JSON label file (`slot.json`) via `readSlotRecord(workspaceRoot)`.
2. Checks whether `record.sessionId === this.id` — i.e. whether the label says the slot file belongs to *this* session.
3. If it matches, calls `slotRestore(filename)` on the llama.cpp client, which tells the server to load that `.bin` file into a slot.
4. If the label names a different session (or the file is missing/corrupt), it falls through to normal prefill.

The label (`slot.json`) stores `{ sessionId, savedAt, tokens }` — a pointer from the single slot file to whichever session last saved.

### Why exactly one file per workspace (not one per session)

The comment in `slot-record.ts` (lines 14–20) explains it directly:

- llama.cpp's `--slot-save-path` takes a **plain filename**, never a path. PrivateCode doesn't know the directory the server was pointed at, so it can't enumerate or delete what the server saved — it must pick the filename itself.
- A slot state is huge: **~23 MiB per 1,000 tokens** (~2.3 GB for a 100k-token state). One file per session that ever existed would be unbounded disk growth.
- So there is **one `.bin` file per workspace**, overwritten on each save. The `slot.json` label is the pointer that says "this file currently holds session X's state." When you open a different session in the same workspace, the old label is swapped out and the new session's state overwrites the `.bin` file on its next save.

The filename itself is deterministic: `privatecode-<12 hex chars>.bin`, where the 12 chars are the first 12 hex digits of `SHA-1(lowercased(workspaceRoot))` — so the same workspace always maps to the same slot filename.

The RPC method is **`git.locate`**, implemented in **`core/src/host/git-rpc.ts`** (lines 246–258).

### How it works

When the user right-clicks a file in the Git tab (or any file tab), the app calls `git.locate` with the file's workspace-addressed path. The handler does four things:

1. **Resolves the workspace path** — calls `resolvePanelPath(workspace, p.path)` in `core/src/host/repos.ts` to turn the panel's path (which may be relative or prefixed with a mount name in a multi-folder workspace) into a canonical absolute path.
2. **Finds the repository root** — calls `repoRootFor(abs)` in `core/src/host/repos.ts`, which walks up the directory tree from the file's parent directory and runs `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` at each level. The walk-up handles deleted files whose parent directory may no longer exist.
3. **Verifies workspace membership** — calls `allowedRoot(workspace, found)` to ensure the discovered root is either the toplevel of a writable workspace mount or a nested repository inside one, rejecting anything outside the workspace.
4. **Returns both spellings** — the canonical repository root and the repository-relative path, so the caller can open history or blame views using git's own naming.

If any step fails, it returns `{ root: null, repoPath: null }` rather than throwing, and the app shows a toast that the file is not in a git repository.

The protocol types are defined in **`core/src/host/git-protocol.ts`** (lines 125–128):

```ts
export interface GitLocateParams { path: string }
export interface GitLocateResult { root: string | null; repoPath: string | null }
```

The app-side callers that invoke this on right-click are in **`app/src/panels/tree.tsx`** (inside `openGitView`, lines 717–736) and **`app/src/App.tsx`** (inside `openGitViewFor`, lines 373–382).
